judgments.forked_readings_summary:
All four readings describe the same task: scaffold a brand-new (net-new, not migration) .NET 10 ASP.NET Core OrderStatus API with EXACTLY one endpoint GET /v1/orders/{orderId}/status, bearer-token auth, a typed HttpClient FulfillmentClient as the data source (no database/persistence), a camelCase {orderId, status, updatedAt} success body, and a {success, errors:[]} envelope for failures. They agree on every load-bearing behavior: 401 on missing/invalid token before the handler, status fetched only from the downstream FulfillmentClient, failures returning the structured envelope, exactly one endpoint with NO list/pagination, and — notably — all four independently and identically resolve the subtle point that the 200 success body is the bare object NOT wrapped in the {success,errors} envelope (the envelope is error-only). All four also share the bearer-auth reading (inbound JWT bearer VALIDATION, with the downstream/outbound OAuth token scheme treated as an unspecified ADAPT/optional point) and the options-with-validation + AddStandardResilienceHandler pattern from the repo's generation spec.

The only divergence is level-of-detail on operational/scaffolding extras, not task identity: Readings 1 and 4 firmly enumerate a Dockerfile (non-root, port 8080), /health + /ready endpoints, log sanitization, and a test project (happy-path + error coverage) as IN-SCOPE deliverables, with reading 4 also naming the explicit scaffold-api phases (Phase 1 design approval, Phase 2 verbatim-paste generation, Stage 1 review loop). Readings 2 and 3 are more minimal — they treat Dockerfile/health/tests as generation-spec defaults or assumptions rather than firm in-scope items, and reading 3 is most explicit about specific status-code mapping (404 not-found, 503 downstream-unavailable). These differences would yield essentially the same artifact; they reflect how much of the standard generation-spec scaffolding each engineer pulled into the firm in-scope list versus left as an assumed default. No material fork.

All four readings describe the SAME task with no material fork. Every interpretation converges on: a net-new .NET 10 (net10.0) ASP.NET Core OrderStatus API; EXACTLY ONE endpoint GET /v1/orders/{orderId}/status with list/pagination explicitly excluded; a bearer-token-authenticated endpoint (401 on missing/invalid token before business logic); a typed HttpClient FulfillmentClient (IFulfillmentClient + FulfillmentClient via AddHttpClient) as the SOLE data source with NO database/persistence; a camelCase JSON success body {orderId, status, updatedAt}; and a {success, errors:[]} error envelope used for failure paths only (all four explicitly note success body is the bare object, NOT wrapped). They share the same comparison surfaces: endpoint/route, auth middleware, wire-format/serialization, downstream client, options/config, Program.cs composition root, and error mapping. They even share the same nuanced assumptions: bearer = JWT validation (not minting), updatedAt = ISO-8601 DateTimeOffset, status = pass-through string, downstream-auth/token-provider treated as an optional ADAPT point, and they would follow examples/generation-specs/dotnet-service.md.

The only differences are minor scope-detail emphasis, not task identity: (1) Readings 1 and 4 explicitly list a test project + Dockerfile + health/ready + log sanitization as in-scope deliverables and explicitly mention running the scaffold-api/Stage 1 self-review loop; Readings 2 and 3 treat tests, Dockerfile, and health endpoints as 'standard scaffold output / not explicitly requested but included' — same artifacts, framed as assumed-extras rather than enumerated requirements. (2) Reading 3 commits to specific failure-to-status-code mappings (downstream -> 503, not-found -> 404) while others leave the downstream-failure code looser. (3) Reading 1 alone explicitly states 'no push/commit/PR unless asked.' These are verbosity/inclusion-threshold differences around peripheral scaffold artifacts (tests, Dockerfile, ops endpoints), not disagreements about what the service IS or does. The core deliverable, surfaces, and behavior are identical across all four.

All four readings describe the same task: scaffold a net-new (non-migration) .NET 10 OrderStatus API with EXACTLY ONE bearer-authenticated endpoint GET /v1/orders/{orderId}/status that fetches status from a downstream typed-HttpClient FulfillmentClient (no DB / no persistence), returns a bare camelCase {orderId, status, updatedAt} success body, and uses a {success, errors[]} envelope for failures — driven through the scaffold-api flow with a Stage 1 self-review loop and no push/commit/PR unless asked.

Surfaces are identical across all four (endpoint/route, camelCase wire-format, bearer auth + authorize, typed HttpClient FulfillmentClient + resilience, options-with-validation, Program.cs DI composition root, error-envelope mapping). Core behavior is in lockstep — including the same subtle, independently-reached reading that the success body is the bare object and the {success,errors} envelope applies to errors ONLY (not a {success,data} wrap), that 401 fires before business logic, and that list/pagination is explicitly excluded. All four also share the same key assumption that 'bearer auth' = inbound JWT/bearer token VALIDATION (authority/audience from config), NOT the outbound OAuth client_credentials TokenProvider pattern from the generation spec, which they omit by default.

The only divergences are depth-of-detail, not task-meaning: (1) Readings 1 and 4 explicitly list Dockerfile (non-root, port 8080), /health + /ready endpoints, and a test project as in-scope, while readings 2 and 3 treat these as spec-default assumptions/optional — but all four would emit the same artifacts because the generation spec mandates them for a net-new service. (2) Failure-to-HTTP-status mapping: reading 3 commits to specific codes (downstream→503, not-found→404, missing-token→401); readings 1/2/4 mention 404/401 and route other failures through the envelope without pinning 503. This is an implementation-detail variation within an agreed behavior (all failures use the envelope), not a fork.
